result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.bonacich_power_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Get Bonacich power centrality for each node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L16222-L16395){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.bonacich_power_centrality( beta=0.1, normalized=False, attr_name=None, return_dict=False ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Bonacich power centrality generalizes eigenvector centrality to capture both cooperative and competitive network dynamics. The key innovation is the β parameter, which controls whether neighbors' power increases (+β) or decreases (-β) a node's own power. The centrality is computed as: `c(α, β) = α(I - βA)^(-1) A 1` where `A` is the adjacency matrix, `α` is a scaling parameter (set automatically), `β` controls the nature of relations, and `1` is a vector of ones. `β > 0`: cooperative relations: being connected to powerful nodes makes you powerful (e.g., collaboration networks, social influence, information diffusion) `β < 0`: competitive relations: being connected to weak nodes makes you powerful (e.g., exchange networks, competitive markets, bargaining power) `β = 1/λ_max`: equivalent to eigenvector centrality The magnitude of `|β|` controls how far influence propagates through the network. Larger `|β|` values mean distant nodes have more influence; a smaller `|β|` localizes influence. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [beta]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.1]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The decay/attenuation parameter. Controls the nature and reach of influence. See the *Details on the beta Parameter* section for more information on settings. [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The normalization method. With `False`, we get L2 normalization where `sum(c^2) = n`, making `c=1` the 'middle' value. Using `True` results in a sum normalization where `sum(c) = 1` (probability distribution). [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name for the node attribute to store results. If not provided, auto-generates name from method name (`bonacich_power_centrality`). [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns dictionary of results. If `False`, stores results as node attributes and returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to centrality scores. If `return_dict=` is `False`: returns self for method chaining. The interpretation depends on `β`: (1) when `β > 0` higher scores = more powerful due to powerful neighbors, and (2) when `β < 0` higher scores = more powerful due to weak neighbors. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [RuntimeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `(I - βA)` is singular. This happens when `β` is too close to `1/λ_max`. Try reducing `|β|` or choosing a different value. ::: ## Details On The Beta Parameter {.doc-details-on-the-beta-parameter} The `beta=` should usually be given a value between `-0.5` to `0.5`. Here's a breakdown on the effect of the `β` value: - `β > 0`: Cooperative (powerful neighbors -> more power) - `β < 0`: Competitive (weak neighbors -> more power) - `β = 0`: Reduces to simple degree centrality ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} - **Algorithm**: uses matrix inversion via LU decomposition to solve `(I - βA)x = A1` - **Time complexity**: `O(n³)` for dense graphs due to matrix operations - **Space complexity**: `O(n²)` to store the adjacency matrix - **Numerical stability**: the algorithm may fail if `β` is too close to `1/λ_max`, where `λ_max` is the largest eigenvalue of `A`. Choose `|β| < 0.9/λ_max` for safety. - **β selection**: there's no universal "correct" `β` value; it should be chosen based on theory and the specific application. - **Negative β instability**: centrality can be more sensitive to `β` changes when `β < 0` compared to `β > 0`. Test multiple values. - **Directed graphs**: works for both directed and undirected graphs. In directed graphs, the interpretation relates to in-degree influence patterns. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Cooperative network (`β > 0`) star graph: ::: {#7772a3c0 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Create star: center connected to 3 leaves g = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_node(label="center") .add_node(label="leaf1") .add_node(label="leaf2") .add_node(label="leaf3") .add_edge(source="center", target="leaf1") .add_edge(source="center", target="leaf2") .add_edge(source="center", target="leaf3") ) # Cooperative: powerful neighbors increase your power power = g.bonacich_power_centrality(return_dict=True, beta=0.1) # center will have highest centrality (connected to many) ``` ::: Competitive network (`β < 0`) exchange network: ::: {#2298c08e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # In exchange/bargaining networks, connecting to weak partners # gives you more bargaining power g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_node(label="D") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") g.add_edge(source="B", target="C") g.add_edge(source="C", target="D") # Negative beta: weak neighbors increase your power power = g.bonacich_power_centrality(return_dict=True, beta=-0.2) # End nodes (A, D) have higher power, so, fewer alternatives ``` ::: Compare with eigenvector centrality: ::: {#2125e738 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # β near 1/λ_max approximates eigenvector centrality # For small graphs, λ_max ≈ max_degree, so try β ≈ 1/max_degree g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_node(label="D") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B") g.add_edge(source="B", target="C") g.add_edge(source="B", target="D") max_deg = max(g.get_degree(node=nid) for nid in g.get_node_ids()) bonacich = g.bonacich_power_centrality(return_dict=True, beta=0.9/max_deg) eigen = g.eigen_centrality() # Should be similar ``` :::
